I throw my tiredness far away

我把疲惫远远抛在身后

cosmopolitan. Belonging to all parts of the world; not restricted to any one country or its inhabitants.
属于世界所有地方；不限于任何一国或其居民。
specific. Having a special determining quality.
具有特殊的、决定性的品质。

It is not necessary to have traveled to imagine oneself as cosmopolitan. To be cosmopolitan is to cast off parochialism in order to reach out to the world. All over “affluent Asia,” emergent classes of professionals, managers, and technical workers have fashioned themselves in relation to an imagined worldliness that reaches across oceans and cultures toward a beckoning global future.

During Indonesia’s “economic miracle” years in the 1980s and 1990s, as foreign money flowed into the country, self-consciously cosmopolitan projects blossomed. Yet these projects were neither homogeneous nor variations on the same design. There were many reasons to reach for the cosmopolitan: for internationally effective political action, for worldly consumption, to facilitate foreign investment, to create charismatic personal identities, to reach transnational professional compatibility, or to achieve broad-ranging scientific or civilizational knowledge. Lawyers demanded internationally recognizable forms of law. McDonalds and Dunkin’ Donuts became fashionable places to eat. Activists agitated for universal human rights. Corporations extended trade agreements. Rayon dresses and pants replaced sarongs in women’s fashion. Environmentalists joined global networks. Nature lovers went camping with the latest outdoor equipment. These varied cosmopolitanisms spoke with and against each other, but not with a single voice. Each was caught up in the desires and promises of its own contingent formation.
想象自己具有世界主义身份并不需要真的旅行过。成为世界主义者，就是抛弃狭隘，向世界伸出双臂。在整个“富庶亚洲”，新兴的专业人士、管理者和技术工人阶层，都参照一种想象的世界眼光来塑造自己，这种世界眼光跨越海洋与文化，伸向一个召唤中的全球未来。

印尼20世纪80年代和90年代的“经济奇迹”岁月，随着外国资金流入，自觉的世界主义项目繁荣起来。然而这些项目既不同质，也不是同一设计的变体。追求世界主义的原因很多：为了国际上有效的政治行动，为了具有世界眼光的消费，为了便利外国投资，为了创造有魅力的个人身份，为了达到跨国专业兼容，或为了获得广泛的科学或文明知识。律师要求国际可识别的法律形式。麦当劳和唐恩都乐成为时髦的用餐地点。活动家鼓动普遍人权。公司扩展贸易协定。人造丝连衣裙和长裤取代纱笼，成为女性时尚。环保主义者加入全球网络。自然爱好者带着最新户外装备去露营。这些不同的世界主义彼此对话、彼此对抗，但并非只有一种声音。每一个都卷入自身偶然形成的欲望与承诺。

The specificity of these cosmopolitanisms is an important object—even a model—for the cultural analysis of knowledge. Cultural analysis thrives on the description of specificity, for it is an appreciation of cultural specificity that best gives us a critical distance from the common-sense platitudes and everyday assumptions of our lives, as well as the powerful ideologies that keep us in their thrall. Yet classically the study of cultural specificity has been identified with the study of small, enclosed places: the diverse “cultures” of an imagined precontact world. For several decades now, scholars studying cultural specificity have moved away from a “tribal” model of cultural difference to look at much larger cultural units, such as nations, ethnic diasporas, and even international projects such as capitalism or human rights. Yet smallness was not the problem of studies of ethnic groups and “isolated” cultures; the problem was the assumption of the autonomous self-generation of culture, and this assumption can plague studies of large units as well as small. Even the most out-of-the-way cultural niches are formed in world-crossing dialogues (Tsing 1993). Cultures are always both wide-ranging and situated, whether participants imagine them as global or local, modern or traditional, futuristic or backward looking. The challenge of cultural analysis is to address both the spreading interconnections and the locatedness of culture. To study a self-conscious cosmopolitanism in all its energizing connections to the world and all its exotic distinctiveness models the inextricability of interconnection and location. It is in this spirit that I turn to Indonesian nature lovers, pencinta alam, and the both familiar and surprising ways they have learned to love nature.

“Nature lovers” are members of student clubs devoted to outdoor activities, such as camping, mountain climbing, rafting, and scuba diving. As participants in internationally recognized adventure sports, they are selfconsciously cosmopolitan in the fashioning of their identities. The nature they learn to love is not the fields and forests of ordinary, parochial, rural lives. As they learn to love nature, student nature lovers break away from the world of routine and authority to embrace the breadth and freedom of the outdoors. The outdoors is made modern, technical, and scientific; it must be taught in classes and taken into one’s own practice through discipline and experience. The cosmopolitanism of nature lovers results from a training of internal agency, desire, and identity; it is a matter of crafting selves. Unlike tourists or migrants, most nature lovers have never been abroad; unlike scientists and other professionals, their work does not require certification. My questions about the specificity of cosmopolitanism turn, here, to the formation of identities and desires. For this, I trace the lineages of knowledge and desire through which the cosmopolitan appreciation or “loving” of nature comes into being. I am also concerned with the cultural specificity of “nature.”

这些世界主义的特殊性是知识文化分析的重要对象——甚至是典范。文化分析靠特殊性描述而兴盛，因为正是对文化特殊性的欣赏，最能给我们批判性距离，远离日常生活的常识陈词与日常假设，以及把我们束缚住的强大意识形态。然而，文化特殊性的研究经典上与对小而封闭地方的研究联系在一起：一个想象中的前接触世界的多样“文化”。几十年来，研究文化特殊性的学者已经从文化差异的“部落”模式转向大得多的文化单位，如国家、族裔散居，甚至资本主义或人权这样的国际项目。然而，小并不是族群和“孤立”文化研究的问题；问题是文化自主自生的假设，而这个假设同样困扰对大型单位的研究。即使最偏僻的文化生态位，也是在跨越世界的对话中形成的（Tsing 1993）。文化总是既广泛又情境化的，无论参与者把它们想象为全球还是地方、现代还是传统、未来主义还是向后看。文化分析的挑战在于同时处理不断扩散的相互联系与文化的位置性。研究一种自觉的世界主义，考察其与世界一切令人振奋的联系及其一切异域独特性，示范了相互联系与位置性如何不可分离。本着这种精神，我转向印尼自然爱好者（pencinta alam），转向他们学会热爱自然的既熟悉又令人惊讶的方式。

“自然爱好者”是致力于户外活动的学生俱乐部成员，活动如露营、登山、漂流和水肺潜水。作为国际公认冒险运动的参与者，他们在塑造身份上自觉是世界主义的。他们学会热爱的自然，不是普通而局限于一地的乡村生活的田野和森林。当学生自然爱好者学会热爱自然时，他们脱离日常与权威的世界，拥抱户外的广阔与自由。户外被弄得现代、技术化、科学化；它必须在课程中被教授，并通过纪律和经验进入自己的实践。自然爱好者的世界主义由内在能动性、欲望和身份的培训产生；是塑造自我的事情。与游客或移民不同，大多数自然爱好者从未出过国；与科学家和其他专业人士不同，他们的工作不需要认证。我关于世界主义特殊性的问题在此转向身份与欲望的形成。为此，我追溯知识与欲望的谱系，世界主义的自然欣赏或“热爱”经由这些谱系而产生。我也关心“自然”的文化特殊性。

I first became interested in Indonesian nature lovers when I interviewed environmental activists, and many told me that they began as student nature lovers. Aristides Katoppo, a well-known environmental journalist, told a story that was echoed in various ways by many environmentalists:
我最早对印尼自然爱好者产生兴趣，是在采访环保活动家时，许多人告诉我他们最初是学生自然爱好者。著名环境记者阿里斯蒂德斯·卡托波讲了一个故事，许多环保主义者以各种方式呼应：
I am a journalist. I also used to be an avid hiker, associated with Mapala UI, the organization of student nature lovers of the University of Indonesia....
我是记者。我也曾是个热衷的徒步者，与印尼大学学生自然爱好者组织 Mapala UI 有关……

Well, climbing the mountains, hiking there: At that time the concept of environment was alien. But going up the mountain slope, it’s quite different if you walk under the canopy, it’s cool. If you walk through a devastated forest the same distance, say you walk half an hour, but it drains a lot of your energy because you can feel the hot sun. I realized that the forest line was receding. I may have seen it for a long time, but at some stage it shocks you. It was receding like the hair of my head! [He laughs.] And I realized that the camping sites where we used to camp where there was clean water available year round had begun to dry up, or else there was a big flood. And other things, such as the disappearance of birds. I think it was in the late 1960s or early 1970s there was a long spell of droughts, and I could see the water supply for the sawah rice fields dry up. Today [1994] you can also see the parched fields, which I knew from other times with water flowing and beautifully green...
Gradually I became more aware of what is now called the environment.

嗯，爬山，在那里徒步：那时环境这个概念还很陌生。但走上山坡，在树冠下行走感觉完全不同，很凉爽。如果你走过一片被毁的森林，同样的距离，比如说走半小时，但它会耗尽你很多精力，因为你能感到烈日。我意识到森林线在后退。也许我已看了很久，但在某个阶段它震撼了你。它像我的头发一样在后退！[他笑了。]我意识到我们过去露营的地点——那里全年有干净水源——开始干涸，或者发生大洪水。还有其他事情，比如鸟的消失。我想那是20世纪60年代末或70年代初，有一段长期干旱，我能看到稻田的水源干涸。今天[1994年]，你也能看到龟裂的田地，而我从其他时候知道那里水流淌、美丽翠绿……
渐渐地，我越来越意识到现在所谓的环境。

To become an environmentalist, Katoppo reminded me, one must learn to recognize and care about “the environment.” His story encouraged me to ask myself, “What is this environment that activists recognize?” Katoppo tells us: The environment is that form of nature that is vulnerable to humanmade devastation and disaster. He was able to recognize it because of shock: The cool forests he had once known had been transformed into hot earth; the streams were drying up. And he experienced the shock because he had hiked through those cool forests and seen those green fields before, as a nature lover, an admirer of nature’s beauty. The romance of nature gives grandeur and autonomy to the natural world; those who appreciate that grandeur are also able to feel the shock of nature’s desecration and destruction. Is it possible, I wondered, that, even in Indonesia, the romance of nature is one important route to an appreciation of nature’s fragility?

卡托波提醒我，要成为环保主义者，一个人必须学会识别并关心“环境”。他的故事鼓励我问自己：“活动家所识别的这个环境是什么？”卡托波告诉我们：环境是那种易受人为破坏和灾难伤害的自然形式。他能够识别它，是因为震惊：他曾经熟悉的凉爽森林已变成灼热土地；溪流正在干涸。他经历这种震惊，是因为他作为自然爱好者、自然美的欣赏者，曾经徒步穿过那些凉爽森林，见过那些绿色田野。自然的浪漫赋予自然世界壮丽与自主性；那些欣赏这种壮丽的人也能感受到自然被亵渎和毁灭的震惊。我想，即使在印尼，自然的浪漫是否也可能是认识自然脆弱性的重要途径？

The idea that the romance of nature might be a significant feature of Indonesian national culture works against every stereotype of the difference between the global north and the global south. The notion of a transcendent nature, separated from culture, is often cited as a unique feature of “the West.” Southerners are supposed to be practical users of nature, interested in feeding themselves but not in admiring wilderness.

Yet in the 1980s and 1990s, nature loving was one of the most popular activities of students all across Indonesia. In every city and provincial town I visited, I kept running into nature lovers without looking for them. Furthermore, there was a selfconscious national consistency about nature loving: student nature lovers across the country learned similar ways of talking about and being in nature. This national consistency was not intended to be indigenous; nature lovers strove to learn international ways of enjoying and appreciating nature. In the process, however, they made these international standards distinctly identifiable as Indonesian by incorporating them into Indonesian nationalisms as well as Indonesian internationalisms.
自然的浪漫可能是印尼民族文化的重要特征，这一想法与全球北方和南方差异的每一种刻板印象相悖。一种超越的、与文化分离的自然观念，常被引为“西方”的独特特征。南方人被认为只是自然的实际使用者，关心喂饱自己，而不关心欣赏荒野。

然而在20世纪80年代和90年代，自然之爱是印尼各地学生最受欢迎的活动之一。在我访问的每个城市和地方城镇，我都不必刻意寻找就不断遇到自然爱好者。此外，自然之爱有一种自觉的全国范围的一致性：全国的学生自然爱好者学习相似的谈论自然和在自然中存在的方式。这种全国范围的一致性并非旨在体现本土传统；自然爱好者努力学习的，是享受和欣赏自然的国际方式。然而在此过程中，他们把这些国际标准纳入印尼民族主义和印尼国际主义，使其明显可识别为印尼的。

Indonesian nature loving thus raises questions about the ways widely circulating knowledges become local. If Indonesian nature loving draws, as it self-consciously does, from international figures and their legacies—Alexander Humboldt, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Sir Edmund Hilary, John Muir, Robert Baden-Powell, Teddy Roosevelt, and many more—how does it become Indonesian? This is the question of cosmopolitan specificity, the subject of this chapter. To address it, I first explore the concept: How does cosmopolitan specificity come about? This allows me to imagine Indonesian nature loving at the confluence of a number of cultural lineages that, taken together, give popular force to both its cosmopolitan yearnings and its locally distinctive features.

因此，印尼的自然之爱提出了广泛流通的知识如何地方化的问题。如果说印尼的自然之爱如它自觉的那样，汲取国际人物及其遗产——亚历山大·洪堡、拉尔夫·沃尔多·爱默生、埃德蒙·希拉里爵士、约翰·缪尔、罗伯特·贝登堡、泰迪·罗斯福等等——它如何变得印尼化？这就是世界主义特殊性的问题，也是本章的主题。为了处理它，我首先探讨这个概念：世界主义特殊性是如何产生的？这让我能够把印尼的自然之爱想象为若干文化谱系的汇流，这些谱系合在一起，赋予其世界主义渴望与地方独特性以大众力量。

Above us rose the volcanic cone of Mt. Merapi. We passed through gorges lined with tropical vines where we touched heart-shaped aroid leaves as big as picture windows and exclaimed at blooming trees with monkeys jumping in the branches. Yet on both sides of the main trail, the trees were straightboled, evenly spaced, and park-like in their orderliness, with cleared ground between them. Pure stands of pines further interrupted my stereotypes of the tropics. I guessed we were in an old tree plantation. My fellow hikers, students from the city, didn’t know. From the beginning, then, I felt disoriented, confused between the strange and the familiar in my appreciation of nature.
我们上方升起默拉皮火山的锥体。我们穿过两旁长满热带藤蔓的峡谷，触摸像大幅观景窗一样大的心形天南星科叶子，惊叹于开花的树木和枝头跳跃的猴子。然而，主径两侧的树木笔直、间距均匀、排列如公园般整齐，树间地面已被清理。纯松林进一步打破了我对热带的刻板印象。我猜我们在一片老的人工林。我的徒步同伴，来自城市的学生，不知道。从一开始，我在对自然的欣赏中就感到迷失方向，在陌生与熟悉之间困惑。

Every now and then we passed an elderly, wrinkle-faced peasant, bent over completely at the waist and balancing a load of grass or wood that far exceeded the size of his or her frail body. But my companions carried frame packs and wore hiking boots and fashionable trousers with extra pockets on the outside for gear. We had even brought a guitar so that we could sing folk songs, in Indonesian and English, at night under the stars. Like the other hiking parties we passed on the trail, ours included men and women. And in common with them too, our party included a young woman who wore the modest jilbab headcovering that signals a personal commitment to Islam. The jilbab covers the forehead and sides of the face and flows down over the shoulders so that no hair is revealed; it does not get in the way of hiking, camping in a gender-mixed group, or staying up late to lie on one’s back to watch the night sky. Combined with jeans and T-shirts or colorful tie-dyes, it added to the self-conscious cosmopolitanism of our group. None of us—Indonesian or American—imagined ourselves to be anything like the peasant women we stopped to watch as they intoned communal chants in their hard labor of digging and carrying sand from the stream bed, with their skirts tucked up around their thighs. Watching but not joining them, we were menikmati alam bebas, enjoying wild and free nature.

我们不时经过一个满脸皱纹的老农，腰弯得很低，平衡着一捆远超其虚弱身体大小的草或木柴。但我的同伴背着框架背包，穿着登山靴和外侧有额外口袋装装备的时髦长裤。我们甚至带了一把吉他，以便夜里在星空下唱印尼语和英语的民歌。像我们在小径上遇到的其他徒步队伍一样，我们队伍里有男有女。与他们也一样，我们队伍里有一位年轻女子，戴着表示个人笃信伊斯兰教的端庄头巾（jilbab）。头巾遮住额头和脸侧，垂下盖住肩膀，不露出头发；它不妨碍徒步、男女混合露营，或熬夜仰卧观看夜空。结合牛仔裤和T恤或彩色扎染，它增添了我们群体自觉的世界主义。我们中没有谁——印尼人或美国人——把自己想象成我们停下来观看的那些农妇：她们在从溪床挖沙、背沙的艰苦劳动中吟诵集体歌谣，裙子卷到大腿。我们观看而不加入，我们在 menikmati alam bebas，享受狂野自由的自然。

Since the mid-1960s, students in Indonesia have been attracted to internationally popular outdoor activities. They have formed themselves into clubs that identify them as pencinta alam, nature lovers. By the 1990s, most every university had multiple nature lovers’ clubs, organized by administrative units such that the law school, agricultural college, literature faculty, or biology department each had their own nature lovers. Many high schools and even middle schools had nature lovers’ clubs. I took the camping trip I have been describing with an informal group of senior university-level nature lovers.
自20世纪60年代中期以来，印尼学生被国际上流行的户外活动吸引。他们组成俱乐部，把自己标识为 pencinta alam，自然爱好者。到20世纪90年代，几乎每所大学都有多个自然爱好者俱乐部，按行政单位组织，法学院、农学院、文学院或生物系各有自己的自然爱好者。许多高中甚至初中也有自然爱好者俱乐部。我描述的这次露营，是与一群非正式的高年级大学自然爱好者一起进行的。

Nature lovers’ clubs recruit students through school activities’ fora; they demand a rigorous training before the student can join as a full member of the club. Short courses are offered on outdoor activities: backpacking, mountaineering, rock climbing, spelunking, kayaking, white-water rafting, scuba diving, hang gliding, survival, orienteering, search and rescue. A course of reading assignments and lectures is followed by practical training under the supervision of seniors, The student initiates graduate as a cohort (angkatan) within the club; each cohort is given a distinctive name. Members then organize activities, ranging from weekend trips to month-long ekspedisi, expeditions. Expeditions combine research, exploration, and adventure. Sometimes the members participate in competitions or in joint training or research with other outdoor-oriented organizations, including the armed forces. When students graduate, they usually leave the group, although sometimes over a prolonged period. Some graduates have started private nature lovers’ clubs for those not associated with schools; the majority of nature lovers, however, are students.

自然爱好者俱乐部通过学校活动论坛招募学生；他们要求学生经过严格训练，才能成为俱乐部正式成员。短期课程涵盖户外活动：背包旅行、登山、攀岩、洞穴探险、皮划艇、白水漂流、水肺潜水、悬挂滑翔、生存、定向越野、搜救。课程包括阅读作业和讲座，随后在高年级成员监督下进行实践训练。入会学生按同一届（angkatan）集体结业，每一届在俱乐部内获得一个独特名称。成员随后组织活动，从周末旅行到为期一个月的 ekspedisi 探险。探险结合研究、探索和冒险。有时成员参加比赛，或与其他户外导向组织——包括武装部队——联合训练或研究。学生毕业时通常离开团体，尽管有时会延续很长一段时间。一些毕业生为不隶属学校的人创办了私人自然爱好者俱乐部；然而大多数自然爱好者是学生。

Nature lovers form tight-knit social groups and networks. The clubs try to locate themselves in an office space that they can use day and night, and members show up at all hours to socialize, sleep, play music, make new friends, and discuss upcoming and past adventures. They raise money together for trips. They survive harrowing experiences together, worry through problems of identity and spiritual focus, and make passionate attachments. For many students, nature lovers’ groups become a home away from home. In their sociality as well as their adventures, nature lovers’ groups open the possibilities of a new social and cultural world, unlike that of childhood. One young woman told me of her sense of self-awakening among nature lovers, saying, “I was quiet at home, but when I went to college, I was like a horse let out on a grassland, like an arrow released from a bow.”

自然爱好者组成紧密的社会群体和网络。俱乐部努力为自己找到可以日夜使用的办公空间，成员随时出现，社交、睡觉、玩音乐、结交新朋友、讨论即将到来和过去的冒险。他们一起为旅行筹钱。他们一起经历惊险遭遇，为身份认同与精神追求的问题反复思量，建立热烈的情感依恋。对许多学生来说，自然爱好者群体成为离家之外的家。在他们的社会性和冒险中，自然爱好者群体开启了新的社会与文化世界的可能性，不同于童年世界。一位年轻女子向我讲述她在自然爱好者中的自我觉醒感，说：“我在家里很安静，但上了大学，我像一匹被放到草原上的马，像一支离弦的箭。”

Some of the college students who join nature lovers’ groups grew up in small towns or even rural areas. But when they leave home, they join a national student culture in which nature has a new form, a new magic. They remake themselves in relation to the beauty, the skills, the danger, and the leadership opportunities of nature loving. It is within this “bubble” context that nature loving develops both its cosmopolitan yearnings and its distinctive specificities. Indonesian nature loving blends characteristics of nature-making projects from around the world: It is part nature romanticism, part scout troop discipline and loyalty, and part commercially sponsored adventure campaign. Yet Indonesian nature lovers are also engaged with a national nature, and one that is further inflected by regional and ethnic nature-loving practices.

加入自然爱好者群体的一些大学生在小城镇甚至农村长大。但当他们离开家，他们加入一种全国学生文化，其中自然有一种新形式、一种新魔力。他们参照自然之爱的美、技能、危险和领导机会重塑自己。正是在这种“泡沫”语境中，自然之爱发展出其世界主义渴望和独特的特殊性。印尼的自然之爱融合了世界各地自然制造项目的特征：部分是自然浪漫主义，部分是童子军的纪律与忠诚，部分是商业赞助的冒险运动。然而印尼自然爱好者也与一种国家化的自然相关，而这种自然又进一步受到区域和族群自然之爱实践的影响。

Nature loving is thus both cosmopolitan and situated. Like a City, it can be appreciated as the hub of many roads, stretching out to other places in every direction; it can also be experienced as an unforgettable and distinctive style, a pace, an outlook, a peculiar arrangement of neighborhoods and markets and parks and crime zones, a manifestation of a particular history that can never be exactly replicated. The closer one looks at any idiosyncratic feature of the city, the more one sees the tracks that lead to other cities in conjoined pasts and presents; the more carefully one follows these links, the more one is startled by the unique features they have given to the city.

因此，自然之爱既是世界主义的，又是情境化的。像一座城市，它可以被欣赏为许多道路的枢纽，向各个方向延伸到其他地方；它也可以被体验为一种难忘而独特的风格、一种节奏、一种景观、一种社区、市场和公园与犯罪地带的奇特排列，一种永远无法被精确复制的特定历史的表现。一个人越仔细看城市的任何独特特征，就越能看到通向其他城市在相互连接的过去与现在中的轨迹；越仔细地跟随这些联系，就越惊讶于它们赋予这座城市的独特特征。

Residents in the city imagine themselves as reaching out to others on many roads; the roads also bring the foreign to them, and they remake it as their own. In its confluence of roads, its bringing together of interconnections, the city becomes most local and specific. In this sense, the confluence is the mode of situating and specifying cosmopolitanism, understood spatially as an appreciation of ideas, things, and beings from many places.
城市居民想象自己沿许多道路向他人伸出；道路也把外来之物带给他们，他们把它重塑为自己的。在道路的汇流中，在相互联系的汇聚中，城市变得最地方、最特殊。在这个意义上，汇流是使世界主义情境化并特殊化的模式，从空间上理解为对来自许多地方的思想、事物和存在的欣赏。

Imagine, too, the history of this confluence over time. Roads have been rerouted, and neighborhoods have changed. The form of the confluence exists only because it is a node of articulation of varied historical trajectories.
也想象一下这种汇流随时间的历史。道路被改道，社区改变。汇流的形式之所以存在，只是因为它是一个多种历史轨迹接合的节点。

Perhaps, in the drive for urban development, office buildings have replaced a neighborhood of squatters; yet the squatters have multiplied and moved into what, before the demise of manufacturing, once was a warehouse district. Looking back from the confluence as we know it today, we might call these shifting urban histories “lineages,” that is, shards of genealogies through which present forms have emerged. Occasionally these lineages result directly from urban planning policies; most of the time, however, they come into existence through some haphazard combination of varied and contradictory planning, unpredictable negotiation, rebellious refusal, and unavoidable confusion. We might speak of “contingent lineages” through which the current form of the city has come into being. The city makes cosmopolitanism its own through these contingent lineages.

也许，在城市发展的驱动下，办公楼取代了擅自占地定居者的社区；但这些占地定居者成倍增加，搬进了制造业消亡之前曾是仓库区的地方。从我们今天所知的汇流回望，我们也许可以把这些变迁的城市历史称为“谱系”，即当前形式借以出现的谱系碎片。偶尔这些谱系直接源于城市规划政策；然而大多数时候，它们通过不同而矛盾的计划、不可预测的协商、叛逆的拒绝和不可避免的混乱之间某种偶然组合而存在。我们也许可以谈论“偶然谱系”，城市当前的形式经由它们而生成。城市通过这些偶然谱系把世界主义变为自己的。

To return from the image of the city to my method of cultural analysis: cosmopolitan specificities can be studied through tracing their contingent lineages. Contingent lineages show us the world-embracing spread of cosmopolitanisms even as they bring us into the articulations through which these cosmpolitanisms become locally identifiable. Like the crossroads and neighborhoods of my city metaphor, the confluences of contingent lineages refigure imported ideas, migrants, and materials from all over the world as local. In these conjunctures, cultures are made and remade.
从城市的意象回到我的文化分析方法：世界主义特殊性可以通过追溯其偶然谱系来研究。偶然谱系向我们展示世界主义拥抱世界的扩散，同时把我们带入这些世界主义变得地方可识别的接合中。像我的城市隐喻中的十字路口和社区一样，偶然谱系的汇流把来自世界各地的进口思想、移民和物质重新塑造为地方性的。在这些接合点中，文化被制造和重新制造。

As I mentioned earlier, the cosmopolitanism of Indonesian nature lovers is a cosmopolitanism of identity formation. Nature lovers are trying to make themselves cosmopolitans. One way to understand this identity project is to consider their reliance on youth as a category through which they simultaneously approach identity formation and cosmopolitanism. Youth is often a time for forging new modes of agency and desire. For nature lovers, this is a resonant frame for creating cosmopolitan knowledge.
如我先前所说，印尼自然爱好者的世界主义是一种身份形成的世界主义。自然爱好者试图把自己造就为世界主义者。理解这一身份项目的一种方式，是考虑他们依靠“青年”这一范畴，同时接近身份形成与世界主义。青年常常是锻造新的能动性和欲望模式的时期。对自然爱好者来说，这是一个为创造世界主义知识而共鸣的框架。

The most difficult thing for “youth” [“pemuda”] is the moment one has to separate one’s rational thoughts from one’s emotions. In an emotional register, I am never going to break free from MG [the nature lovers’ club]. In a rational register, I have to use my time as efficiently as possible.

MG is a home and my first family in Yogya. This organization has already given me and my friends the meaning of comradeship, friendship, enmity, ambition, idealism, knowledge, insight, spirit, a place of protection, the meaning of growing up and of self-enlightenment.
Closeness to “nature” and all of its harmoniousness, its conceit as well as its grandeur, has already truly changed my views of the meaning of life, death, and self.
对“青年”（pemuda）来说，最难的事，是必须把理性思考与情感分开的那一刻。在情感层面，我永远不会脱离 MG（自然爱好者俱乐部）。在理性层面，我必须尽可能高效地利用时间。
MG 是日惹的一个家，是我的第一个家庭。这个组织已经给了我和我的朋友们同志情谊、友谊、敌意、抱负、理想主义、知识、洞见、精神、一个受保护的地方、成长与自我启蒙的意义。
与“自然”的亲近，及其所有和谐、自负与壮丽，已经真正改变了我对生命、死亡与自我意义的看法。

Youth is a self-conscious attribute of the nature lovers I met. In contrast to the U.S. “outdoors” culture of the 1950s and 1960s that I knew from my childhood, Indonesian nature loving is not a family activity. After women have children, they stop participating in nature loving, even if they have enjoyed hiking and camping. In contrast to U.S. nature appreciation, Indonesian nature loving is not a way to bring young and old into the same space. When men graduate and find jobs, they “advise” nature lovers but do not join them in their activities. Although middle-class Indonesians of all ages sometimes engage in outdoor leisure activities, nature lovers’ groups are perceived as bringing together and organizing youth (pemuda).

青年身份是我遇到的自然爱好者自觉认同的属性。与我从童年知道的20世纪50年代和60年代美国“户外”文化不同，印尼的自然之爱不是家庭活动。女性有了孩子后就停止参与自然之爱，即使她们曾享受徒步和露营。与美国的自然欣赏不同，印尼的自然之爱不是把年轻人和老人带入同一空间的方式。男性毕业后找到工作，会“指导”自然爱好者，但不参加他们的活动。虽然各年龄段的中产印尼人有时参与户外休闲活动，自然爱好者群体仍被视为联合和组织青年（pemuda）的场所。

Benedict Anderson (1972) has described how pemuda emerged as a revolutionary force in the 1940s, as Indonesia struggled for independence from colonial rule. The radical youth he describes drew from Javanese traditions in which youth, for men, was a time of wandering in search of utopian and spiritual illumination before the responsibilities of adult status set in. At the end of World War II, youth organized to express the urgency of national independence; they forced their often-recalcitrant elders into stronger confrontations with the European armies and administrators who came to repossess the colony from Japanese occupation. The youth imagined themselves as responsible for the fate of the nation.
本尼迪克特·安德森（1972）描述了20世纪40年代印尼争取摆脱殖民统治独立时，pemuda 如何作为革命力量出现。他描述的那种激进青年借鉴爪哇传统：对男性而言，青年是在成年身份责任到来之前漫游、寻求乌托邦与精神启明的时期。二战结束时，青年组织起来表达民族独立的紧迫性；他们迫使往往不情愿的长辈更强烈地对抗欧洲军队和行政官员——后者来从日本占领手中收回殖民地。青年把自己想象为对国家命运负责。

After Indonesia gained its independence, the youth movement dissipated, only to rise again in 1966, when students took to the streets calling for a radical change in national politics. Calling themselves “the Generation of 1966” in explicit dialogue with the revolutionary “Generation of 1945,” they organized mass demonstrations and demanded a ban on the Indonesian Communist Party, a new cabinet, and a reduction in soaring prices. Working under the protection of the army, and particularly the elite army corps that later became known as Kopassus (at that time RPKAD), students played an important role in ending the regime of Indonesia’s first president, Sukarno, and the transfer of power to then-General Suharto, with his ambitions to create a New Order for Indonesia (Douglas 1970: 153–74). Outside of the universities, Islamic party youth wings were mobilized in the mass killings of suspected communists in which a half million people were killed (Anderson 1999).

印尼获得独立后，青年运动消散，直到1966年再度兴起，当时学生走上街头，要求国家政治发生激进变革。他们自称“1966年一代”，明确与革命的“1945年一代”对话，组织大规模示威，要求取缔印尼共产党、成立新内阁、降低飞涨的物价。在军队保护下——尤其是后来称为 Kopassus 的精锐军团（当时叫 RPKAD）——学生们在结束印尼首任总统苏加诺政权、把权力移交给时任将军苏哈托的过程中发挥了重要作用，后者怀有建立印尼新秩序的野心（Douglas 1970: 153–74）。在大学之外，伊斯兰政党青年翼被动员参加大规模杀害疑似共产党人的行动，共有50万人被杀（Anderson 1999）。

University students and Islamic youth were among the strongest supporters of the New Order in its early years. Slowly, however, their criticisms mounted. A decisive break for students occurred in 1974, when student demonstrations during the visit of the Japanese prime minister embarrassed the government, which responded by clamping down on students and the press. By the end of the decade, the government had decided to shut down all student politics. The 1978 Campus Normalization Law outlawed student organizations. A political quiescence set in that was to last into the early 1990s.
大学生和伊斯兰青年是新秩序早年的最强支持者之一。然而，他们的批评慢慢增多。1974年发生了学生的决定性决裂，当时日本首相访问期间的学生示威让政府难堪，政府回应是压制学生和媒体。到那十年结束时，政府决定关闭一切学生政治。1978年的校园正常化法取缔学生组织。政治沉寂出现，持续到20世纪90年代初。

Meanwhile, James Siegel (1986) has argued, the lineage of youth nationalism passed into the public schools. “Whatever their inadequacies,” Siegel writes, “there can be no doubt that schools today are the places where sentiments of nationalism are centered; when people view youth in terms of the future, as they do frequently and fervently, it is the schools they think about” (1986: 139). The nationalism of schooling is expressed particularly in the use of Indonesian, the national language, in place of regional mother tongues. The use of Indonesian, Siegel argues, writing of the Javanese city of Solo, creates a respectful distance between the student and his or her learning, turning repetitive recitations into revelations of the mystery of the future. Although there is no trace of the revolutionary politics of the 1940s, schooling creates a future-looking nationalism built around the possibilities of youth. Furthermore, by removing the political content of youth nationalism, Siegel argues, the New Order regime opened the way for other kinds of youth culture to emerge.

与此同时，詹姆斯·西格尔（1986）论证，青年民族主义的谱系传入了公立学校。“无论它们有什么不足，”西格尔写道，“毫无疑问，今天的学校是民族主义情感的中心；当人们把青年视为未来时——他们经常而且热烈地这样做——他们想到的是学校”（1986: 139）。学校教育的民族主义尤其表现在使用国语印尼语代替地方母语。西格尔在论述爪哇城市梭罗时论证，使用印尼语在学生与其学习之间制造了一种尊重的距离，把重复的背诵变成对未来的神秘的启示。尽管没有20世纪40年代革命政治的痕迹，学校教育创造了一种以青年可能性为中心的面向未来的民族主义。此外，西格尔论证，通过移除青年民族主义的政治内容，新秩序政权为其他类型的青年文化出现开辟了道路。

The first nature lovers’ clubs formed at the university level in the last years of the Sukarno regime, and as an explicit reaction to the tensions and struggles of the crisis-oriented student politics of the time. The founders of nature lovers’ clubs at the University of Indonesia—many of whom were student activists—decided to create some activities that were decidedly nonpolitical, as they understood politics.

Yet what is nonpolitics? Their ideas for a new youth activity were formulated in the shadow of the youth politics lineage. Where politics was socially boisterous (ramai), they chose the quiet loneliness (sunyi) of nature. Instead of social contention, they chose natural harmony. Their object was shaped by the heritage of “politics” even as they chose to avoid it.
第一批自然爱好者俱乐部在苏加诺政权最后几年形成于大学层面，明确是对当时危机导向学生政治的紧张与斗争的反应。印尼大学自然爱好者俱乐部的创始人——其中许多是学生活动家——决定创造一些按他们对政治的理解明确属于非政治的活动。
然而什么是非政治？他们关于新青年活动的想法是在青年政治谱系的阴影下形成的。政治是社会喧闹（ramai）之处，他们选择自然的安静孤独（sunyi）。他们选择自然和谐，而不是社会争斗。他们的对象由“政治”的遗产塑造，即使他们选择避开它。

Some of these early founders became critics of the Suharto regime; however, their idea was taken up and popularized by new cohorts of students in the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s precisely because it helped to delineate the nonpolitical nationalism of the New Order. Nature loving mirrored the frame of radical youth politics by assuming an enthusiastic nationalism; yet it avoided politics. By turning the legacy of youth politics on its head, nature loving helped formulate what a youthful and cosmopolitan nationalism might mean outside of the contentious political struggles of the 1940s through the 1970s.
这些早期创始人中有些成为苏哈托政权的批评者；然而，他们的想法被20世纪70、80、90年代的一届届新学生接受并普及，恰恰因为它有助于界定新秩序的非政治民族主义。自然之爱通过秉持一种热情的民族主义，映照了激进青年政治的框架；但它避免了政治。通过把青年政治的遗产倒转过来，自然之爱帮助阐明了在20世纪40年代至70年代争论性政治斗争之外，一种年轻的世界主义民族主义可能意味着什么。

Nature lovers were not, however, concerned with the national political trajectory; they were self-consciously politically trivial. They would never have flourished except for the coming together of other meanings of youth from which they gained force. Three other emergent lineages of youthful agency have been important in popularizing nature loving. First, youth found themselves at the cutting-edge of class formation during the New Order. The new middle class depended on cultural distinction, in Pierre Bourdieu’s (1984) sense, to give shape to their economic role as mediators for the influx of international money during the years of Indonesia’s economic “miracle.” Young people—and the education process itself—were credited as the formulators of these cosmopolitan distinctions, which would allow the young to move into a global future imagined as wealthy and successful. Nature lovers’ relearning of “nature” as something transcendent and romantic has been a key distinction for cosmopolitan youth.

然而，自然爱好者并不关心国家政治轨迹；他们自觉地在政治上无足轻重。如果不是青年其他意义的汇合赋予他们力量，他们永远不会繁荣。另外三条新兴的青年能动性谱系对自然之爱的普及很重要。第一，在新秩序期间，青年发现自己处于阶级形成的前沿。新中产阶级依赖皮埃尔·布迪厄（1984）意义上的文化区分，来塑造其作为印尼经济“奇迹”年间国际资金流入中介的经济角色。年轻人——以及教育过程本身——被视为这些世界主义区分的形成者，这些区分将让年轻人进入一个被想象为富裕而成功的全球未来。自然爱好者把“自然”重新学习为超越而浪漫的东西，是世界主义青年的一个关键区分。

Second, nature lovers nationalized a once-foreign youth agenda: They domesticated international adventure tourism, making it their own. In the 1970s, Indonesia became a popular destination for northern tourists. One of the most distinctive forms of international tourism has been adventure tourism: trips to “wild” places imagined as involving physical challenges, unpredictable dangers, and new discoveries. In this spirit, Indonesia hosted foreign jungle trekkers, mountain climbers, and rafting teams. These activities displayed the challenge of youthful identity, as travelers overcame the unknown to find their essential selves. It did not take long for Indonesian students to master these activities and to plot out a domestic scene of adventure tourism that offered opportunities for personal growth without the necessity of foreign travel. By the 1980s, Indonesian nature lovers were mounting expeditions all over the archipelago, forging a new national geography that featured “wild” places and exotically “local” village people to surround their new cosmopolitanism.

第二，自然爱好者把一度外来的青年议程转化为本国的议程：他们把国际冒险旅游驯化，变为自己的。20世纪70年代，印尼成为北方游客的热门目的地。国际旅游最独特的形式之一是冒险旅游：前往被想象为涉及身体挑战、不可预测危险和新发现的“荒野”地方。本着这种精神，印尼接待了外国丛林徒步者、登山者和漂流队。这些活动展示了青年身份的挑战，旅行者克服未知以找到本质自我。印尼学生很快就掌握了这些活动，并规划出一个国内冒险旅游场景，提供个人成长机会而无需出国旅行。到20世纪80年代，印尼自然爱好者正在整个群岛发起探险，锻造一种新国家地理，以“荒野”地方和异域“地方”村民环绕他们的新世界主义。

Third, nature lovers became a particular species of youthful consumers. The students I knew joked and complained about nature lover consumerism. By the 1990s, they said, nature lovers could be identified by their fashionable flannel shirts, jeans, and hiking boots. The nostalgic reminisced about an earlier pre-commercial period; now, they worried, it’s all about fashion, and people don’t respect and care about each other. The freshmen, said the seniors, were too caught up in equipment. But all the nature lovers I knew loved equipment. Their introductory courses diagrammed and explained the importance of backpacks, tents, and camping stoves as well as more specialized climbing gear, kayaking gear and other such items. Small industries sprang up to supply students with Indonesian-made versions of international adventure sports gear. Both domestic and foreign companies began to see the potential of advertising using images of nature lover activities: They could show young, active people challenging the world with the help of their brand-name products.

第三，自然爱好者成为一种特定的青年消费者。我认识的学生开玩笑也抱怨自然爱好者消费主义。他们说，到20世纪90年代，自然爱好者可以通过时髦的法兰绒衬衫、牛仔裤和登山靴辨认。怀旧者回忆更早的前商业时期；他们担心，现在一切都关乎时尚，人们不再相互尊重关心。学长们说，新生太沉迷装备。但我认识的所有自然爱好者都热爱装备。他们的入门课程图解并解释背包、帐篷、露营炉以及更专业的攀登装备、皮划艇装备等的重要性。小工业涌现，为学生供应印尼制造的国际冒险运动装备版本。国内外公司开始看到使用自然爱好者活动形象做广告的潜力：它们可以展示年轻、活跃的人借助其品牌产品挑战世界。

National anti-politics; middle-class distinction; domestic adventure tourism; consumer culture: These four lineages came together to give meaning and practical substance to nature loving as a project for youth. Their routes toward youthful identity overlapped and intertwined, offering the excitement and stability of varied perspectives. Each provided a channel through which cosmopolitanism was made locally workable. These channels formed a confluence at which nature loving reached out to the world—and made worldliness its own. To see how this could be, I offer a closer look at each of these lineages.
国家反政治；中产阶级区分；国内冒险旅游；消费文化：这四条谱系汇合，赋予自然之爱作为青年项目以意义和实践实质。它们通往青年身份的道路重叠交织，提供不同视角的兴奋与稳定。每一条都提供一条渠道，使世界主义在地方变得可行。这些渠道形成一个汇流，自然之爱在此向世界伸出——并把世界眼光变为自己的。为了看看这是如何可能的，我更仔细地考察每一条谱系。

Up and down, ravines and steep slopes, we became used to having our backs bent, while the load of our packs felt heavier because of the previous day’s rain. A hard rain returned to join us as we put up the tents around 4:30 in the afternoon. On the 17th of August, Independence Day, we didn’t forget to have a small ceremony after we finished packing up the camp, and it was affecting enough to have a 17th of August ceremony in the middle of the saddening and lonely forest far from civilization.
上上下下，沟壑与陡坡，我们习惯了弓着背，而前一天的雨让背包显得更重。下午四点半左右，我们搭帐篷时，大雨又回来与我们作伴。8月17日独立日，我们在收好营地后不忘举行一个小仪式，在远离文明的令人悲伤而孤独的森林中举行8月17日仪式，足以令人动容。
—reminiscing about an expedition in a club log book
——回忆一次探险，载于俱乐部日志

New Order nature lovers participated in a nationwide organizational network. They learned to love a national nature, that is, one that was made accessible through their national citizenship and schooling. In the process they learned to be Indonesians. As the opening quotation suggests, this was a heartfelt nationalism and not just a ploy to avoid state repression. Yet it was also a nationalism without either radical urgency or liberal criticism. It was self-consciously empty of a social change-oriented politics. It is perhaps useful, indeed, to think of New Order nature loving, iconically, as an Independence Day celebration in the “lonely forest far from civilization”: an appreciation of the nation from the perspective of its resounding political emptiness.

新秩序的自然爱好者参与全国性组织网络。他们学会热爱一种国家化的自然，即一种通过其国家公民身份和学校教育而可接近的自然。在此过程中，他们学会做印尼人。正如开篇引文所示，这是一种发自内心的民族主义，而不只是避免国家镇压的策略。然而它也是一种既没有激进紧迫性也没有自由主义批判的民族主义。它自觉缺乏以社会变革为导向的政治。实际上，也许可以把新秩序的自然之爱标志性地想象为“远离文明的孤独森林”中的独立日庆典：从其响亮的政治空虚视角对国家的欣赏。

The national frame of nature loving was produced and reproduced in nationwide meetings and training standards, in the everyday practices and assumptions of university student culture, and in dreams of participating in national and international competitions. Every August 17th, New Order nature lovers held demonstrations of agility and solidarity in celebration of Indonesian independence. Meetings, training, competitions, and displays of patriotism brought them into the form-and-routine-conscious world of the state bureaucracy. But many New Order nature lovers also imagined themselves as on the way out the door. For those who knew the freedom and wonder of nature, they told me, these organizational forms were the necessary formalities but not the content of nature loving. Nationalism in their hands became an experience-based love of countryside as much as country. To be outside of politics meant, to them, to be able to escape from regulation, even as state regulation was a necessary form.
“I don’t follow any political activities or any forms of activism at all. With the circle of nature lovers, I run to the mountains.” (DS)

自然之爱的国家框架在全国会议和训练标准中、在大学生文化的日常实践与假设中、在参加全国和国际比赛的梦想中被生产与再生产。每年8月17日，新秩序自然爱好者举行敏捷与团结的展示，庆祝印尼独立。会议、训练、比赛和爱国展示把他们带入国家官僚机构注重形式与常规的世界。但许多新秩序自然爱好者也想象自己在走出门外。他们告诉我，对那些了解自然自由与奇迹的人来说，这些组织形式是必要的形式，但不是自然之爱的内容。在他们手中，民族主义变成一种基于经验的、对乡土和对国家的爱。对他们来说，处于政治之外意味着能够逃离管制，即使国家管制是一种必要形式。
“我完全不参与任何政治活动或任何形式的行动主义。与自然爱好者的圈子一起，我跑向群山。”（DS）

“We were hedonists; we liked to play in free nature. ... We learned from our friends. Our friends were rotten, extremists, ‘against the law.’ It was fun actually.... At that time, nature lovers were identified as ‘outlaws’ [English]: dirty clothes, never bathed, not caring, ‘the important thing is I enjoy it’ [refrain of a popular song]. I had a special uniform: scratched jeans and sometimes I just wore sandals.... We were long-haired; we smoked.” (BPS)
我们曾是享乐主义者；我们喜欢在自由的自然中玩耍……我们向朋友学习。我们的朋友是烂人、极端分子、‘违法者’。其实挺好玩……那时，自然爱好者被认定为‘法外之徒’[英文]：脏衣服，从不洗澡，不在乎，‘重要的是我享受它’[一首流行歌的副歌]。我有一套特别的制服：刮破的牛仔裤，有时我只穿凉鞋……我们留长发；我们抽烟。（BPS）

In this vein, nature lovers gained a reputation as “hippies” (kelompok hippies) and drunkards who did not properly respect adult authority. One of the more popular stories about the origin of nature loving that nature lovers told me was that they took the international scouting model but divorced it from the discipline, regulation, and status hierarchy of scouting to experience nature in all its freedom.

Nature lovers were criticized for their lack of discipline, combined with their interest in activities, such as mountain climbing, that were seen as involving great risk. Students quarreled with their parents over nature lover activities; one of the most difficult moments in trip planning, they said, is getting parental permission.
在这种风气下，自然爱好者获得“嬉皮士”（kelompok hippies）和酒鬼的名声，不尊重成人权威。自然爱好者告诉我的关于自然之爱起源的较流行故事之一是，他们采用国际童子军模式，但把它与童子军的纪律、管制和地位等级分离，以体验自然的全部自由。
自然爱好者因缺乏纪律而受到批评，同时他们感兴趣的活动——如登山——被视为涉及巨大风险。学生因自然爱好者活动与父母争吵；他们说，旅行计划中最困难的时刻之一是获得父母许可。

Even the most compliant of nature lovers were forced into an awkward dance with state authority. In the late 1970s, when all student organizations were shut down as part of the military “normalization” of university campuses, nature lovers were shut down too. In Yogya, where the military raided the university, all student organizations, including nature lovers’ clubs, saw their records burned. Slowly, nature lovers regrouped, this time even more carefully divorced from politics. As one participant of the time recalls, the groups reappeared on a “hobby” basis, avoiding student politics and incorporating regime-initiated rhetoric. By the 1980s, nature lovers’ clubs had become quite popular across the country. But on every significant outing, they needed the permission of police and civil authorities. In the process, nature lovers learned to imagine themselves in a complicated relationship with the state, involving both respect and evasion.

即使最顺从的自然爱好者也被迫与国家权威跳一支尴尬的舞。20世纪70年代末，当所有学生组织作为军方“正常化”大学校园的一部分被关闭时，自然爱好者组织也遭关闭。在日惹，军队突袭大学，包括自然爱好者俱乐部在内的所有学生组织的记录被烧毁。自然爱好者慢慢重新集结，这一次更加小心地与政治分离。正如当时一位参与者回忆，这些团体以“爱好”为基础重新出现，避开学生政治，并纳入政权发起的修辞。到20世纪80年代，自然爱好者俱乐部已在全国相当流行。但每次重要外出，他们都需要警察和民政当局的许可。在此过程中，自然爱好者学会把自己想象为与国家处于复杂关系中，既尊重又回避。

It was in this political atmosphere that nature lovers developed ties with the armed forces. Some nature lovers I spoke to had participated in armysponsored training or competitions, and they recalled the discipline they learned there with considerable pride. In this spirit, too, one contributor to a nature lovers’ 1997 log book wrote an unfavorable comparison between the nature lovers’ club and Kopassus, the elite army unit that only a year later became notorious for firing on student protesters.

The nature lover noted comparable features of nature lovers and Kopassus: Each trains initiates forming cohorts that face challenges together. Yet, the writer concludes, nature lovers suffer in the comparison. Kopassus, with its discipline, spirit, arrogance, and repeated practice, has succeeded in reaching Mount Everest—“something that gives pride to the Indonesian nation.” In contrast, the nature lovers’ club is caught in never-ending internal squabbles and can’t accomplish anything. The entry is intended to revitalize club spirit.
正是在这种政治氛围中，自然爱好者与武装部队发展关系。与我交谈的一些自然爱好者参加过军方赞助的训练或比赛，他们相当自豪地回忆在那里学到的纪律。本着这种精神，一位1997年自然爱好者日志的撰稿人写了一段对自然爱好者俱乐部与 Kopassus 的不利比较。Kopassus 是精锐军队单位，仅一年后因向学生抗议者开枪而臭名昭著。
这位自然爱好者指出自然爱好者与 Kopassus 的可比特征：两者都训练新人组成共同面对挑战的队列。然而，作者得出结论，自然爱好者在此比较中处于下风。Kopassus 凭借纪律、精神、傲慢和反复练习，成功登上了珠穆朗玛峰——“一件给印尼民族带来骄傲的事”。相比之下，自然爱好者俱乐部陷入无休止的内部争吵，什么也做不成。这篇文字旨在重振俱乐部精神。

The log book entry itself, intermingled with late-night stream of consciousness thoughts, reminiscences of past expeditions, romantic nature poetry, exhortations for better performance in competitions, words from popular songs, and caricatures of club members, is not very important. But it does evoke a major arena in which the “anti-politics” patriotism of New Order nationalism was promoted through the collaboration of nature lovers’ clubs and the armed forces: mountain climbing. In international understanding, to scale a mountain peak is to conquer it for the nation. Mountain climbing as “something that gives pride to the Indonesian nation” is a good example of a nationalized cosmopolitanism, that is, a world-embracing standard that enters local notions of nation-making. Here, the armed forces and the nature lovers have needed each other. When the army first became interested in mountain climbing, they learned from the more experienced nature lovers. In turn, army sponsorship has guaranteed the finest equipment, the highest-level permission, and the most spectacular peaks for the nature lovers. Working together, nature lovers and army men have made the national scaling of mountain peaks their own.

日志条目本身——交织着深夜意识流思绪、往次探险回忆、浪漫自然诗、对比赛更好表现的劝勉、流行歌曲歌词和俱乐部成员漫画——并不很重要。但它确实唤起了一个主要场域，新秩序民族主义的“反政治”爱国主义通过自然爱好者俱乐部与武装部队的合作得到推广：登山。在国际理解中，攀登一座山峰就是为国家征服它。登山作为“给印尼民族带来骄傲的事”，是纳入国家框架的世界主义的好例子，即一种进入地方的国家建构观念的世界性标准。在这里，武装部队和自然爱好者彼此需要。军队最初对登山感兴趣时，向更有经验的自然爱好者学习。反过来，军方赞助保证了自然爱好者最好的装备、最高级别的许可和最壮观的山峰。自然爱好者和军人一起，把以国家名义攀登山峰变成了自己的事业。

Mountaineering was the favored sport of the country’s most well known nature lover of the late 1980s and early 1990s, a University of Indonesia student and journalist for the daily paper Kompas who carried the already cosmopolitan-sounding name of Norman Edwin. Edwin popularized nature loving through his newspaper articles. In one series, he chronicled the climb jointly undertaken by the Kopassus mountaineering unit and a team of student nature lovers from Pagata University in April 1990 (Edwin 1990a, 1990b). The party climbed Mount Jaya, the peak in West Papua that had been designated “not only the highest in Indonesia, but also in Southeast Asia and the Pacific” (1990a: 13). The ascent was particularly historic because it recapitulated the first Indonesian climb of this peak in 1964, shortly after the Republic of Indonesia assumed administration of West Papua, in one of thenPresident Sukarno’s more flamboyant nationalist moves.
As Edwin explains it, the 1964 ascent was part of national history as “the first time the highest peak in Indonesia was ‘subjugated’ by sons of Indonesia” (1990a: 1).

登山是20世纪80年代末和90年代初全国最著名自然爱好者的偏爱运动。他是印尼大学学生、《罗盘报》记者，名叫诺曼·埃德温，这个名字听起来已经很有世界主义味道。埃德温通过报纸文章普及自然之爱。在一个系列中，他记录了1990年4月 Kopassus 登山队与帕加塔大学（Pagata University）学生自然爱好者团队联合进行的攀登（Edwin 1990a, 1990b）。队伍攀登查亚峰，这座西巴布亚山峰被指定为“不仅是印尼最高，也是东南亚和太平洋最高”（1990a: 13）。这次登顶尤其具有历史意义，因为它重演了1964年印尼首次攀登此峰；那是在印尼共和国接管西巴布亚行政后不久，属于时任总统苏加诺较为张扬的民族主义举措之一。
正如埃德温所解释，1964年登顶是国家历史的一部分，是“印尼最高峰第一次被印尼之子‘征服’”（1990a: 1）。

The 1964 expedition to what then was called “Mount Sukarno” was plagued with difficulties, and, literally, bogged down in the mud. A forest-and-swamp transect that was supposed to take six days instead took six weeks. The party of climbers continued against all odds in part because Sukarno exhorted them over the radio to complete their task for the motherland. “Continue to advance! No retreat!” he admonished. When three officers stood at the summit to “offer their respect to the nation as a sign of their completed service” (the message they left in a bottle under the Indonesian flag), they felt that their prayers were miraculously answered. In contrast, the 1990 expedition was facilitated by “modern transport”: buses, cable cars, and the dropping of food and supplies by helicopter. “This expedition is simultaneously a military training, so logistic supplies and equipment are carried out with military procedure,” said a Kopassus spokesman. Furthermore, the Kopassus mountain climbing team—unlike the poorly prepared 1964 army climbers—had been in training since 1983, when the unit first contacted student nature lovers for technical assistance. Still, the party experienced their share of challenges. Because improved transportation allowed them to gain altitude so rapidly, many members of the party experienced altitude sickness. Rain and fog put an end to their first attempt to scale the highest peak. Yet on April 15, 1990, the thirty-eighth anniversary of Kopassus’s founding, two Kopassus officers climbed to the top. On the 17th, Kopassus men and nature lovers stood on the peak to remember the earlier expedition: The 1964 climbers “opened the way; now we are continuing their efforts to become military officers who bring about our nation’s national ideals” (1990a: 13).

1964年远征当时称为“苏加诺山”的山峰，困难重重，而且真的陷入泥沼。原定六天穿越森林和沼泽的行程，竟耗时六周。攀登队伍排除万难继续前进，部分原因是苏加诺通过无线电劝勉他们为祖国完成任务。“继续前进！不得后退！”他告诫道。当三名军官站在顶峰“向国家表达敬意，作为他们完成服务的标志”（他们留在印尼国旗下一只瓶子里的信息）时，他们感到祈祷奇迹般地得到了回应。相比之下，1990年的远征得到“现代运输”的便利：巴士、缆车、直升机空投食物和补给。“这次远征同时是一次军事训练，所以后勤补给和装备按军事程序执行，”一位 Kopassus 发言人说。此外，Kopassus 登山队——与准备不足的1964年军队攀登者不同——自1983年以来一直在训练，当时该单位首次联系学生自然爱好者寻求技术援助。不过，队伍也经历了他们那份挑战。由于交通改善让他们如此迅速上升，许多队员出现高山症。雨雾结束了他们第一次攀登最高峰的尝试。然而1990年4月15日，Kopassus 成立38周年，两名 Kopassus 军官登上顶峰。17日，Kopassus 军人和自然爱好者站在峰顶纪念早先的远征：1964年的攀登者“开辟了道路；现在我们继续他们的努力，成为实现我们国家民族理想的军官”（1990a: 13）。

Without a forced march through the mud, the 1990 party could enjoy an efficient and predictable nationalism bathed in the expectation of success. Edwin congratulates the officers on their discipline and camaraderie. Theirs is a success of national culture, which, unlike Sukarno’s mass politics, needs no struggle. They are already dreaming of their next challenge: to go abroad to conquer foreign mountains. “Continue to advance, no retreat!” Edwin echoes Sukarno, referring to their dreams (1990a: 13). But the advances and retreats have changed. Under the protective shadow of the state, mountain climbing offers an opportunity not only for army spectacles but also for individual self-development: technical prowess, athletic strength, personal discipline, and even the admiration of beauty. The prerequisite is that one leave aside public criticism and debate.

无需再在泥沼中艰苦行军，1990年的队伍可以享受一种高效可预测、沐浴在成功期待中的民族主义。埃德温祝贺军官们的纪律与同志情谊。他们的成功是一种民族文化的成功；与苏加诺的大众政治不同，它不需要斗争。他们已经在梦想下一个挑战：出国征服外国山峰。“继续前进，不得后退！”埃德温呼应苏加诺，指他们的梦想（1990a: 13）。但前进与后退已经改变。在国家保护的阴影下，登山不仅为军队奇观提供机会，也为个人自我发展提供机会：技术能力、运动力量、个人纪律，甚至对美的欣赏。前提是一个人搁置公共批评与辩论。
The student nature lovers of the 1980s and 1990s came of age under this protective state shadow.
20世纪80年代和90年代的学生自然爱好者在这片保护性的国家阴影下长大成人。

A story of disgust and village life: Nur went to Bali for a nature lovers’ training, and stayed in a village. When she went down to the river to brush her teeth in the morning, she saw human feces [shit, English] floating by. Before this incident, they had laughed at a team mate who proposed to brush his teeth using bottled water. Afterwards, everyone on the team used bottled water to brush their teeth.
一个关于厌恶和乡村生活的故事：努尔去巴厘岛参加自然爱好者训练，住在一个村庄。早晨她下河刷牙时，看到人类粪便[shit，英文]漂过。在这件事之前，他们还嘲笑一位提议用瓶装水刷牙的队友。之后，队里每个人都用瓶装水刷牙。
—my notes from an interview (in Indonesian except for the word “shit”), 1997
——我的采访笔记（除“shit”一词外均为印尼语），1997

Norman Edwin’s journalism provides an entry point into other aspects of nature lovers’ culture as well. Consider nature lovers’ ideas about rural society. Some nature lovers come from rural backgrounds, but, whether urban or rural, they make themselves urbanites by re-learning nature as an object of modern technology, international standards of training, and transcendent romance. Nature lovers do not go fishing or hunting; those are activities of rural people. They explore, study, subjugate, and admire nature. In the process, they create a set of rural-urban distinctions. In the anecdote from an interview with which I opened this section, a nature lover tells me of her sense of abjection confronting the ordinary conditions of rural life. Through this abjection, she makes herself a stranger in her home country; she approaches the rural with the sophistication, resources, and sense of alienation of a cosmopolitan traveler. This is a process of class formation. Through these cultural distinctions, a cosmopolitan managerial class has fashioned itself.

诺曼·埃德温的新闻工作也为了解自然爱好者文化的其他方面提供了入口。想想自然爱好者关于乡村社会的观念。一些自然爱好者来自乡村背景，但无论城市还是乡村，他们都通过把自然重新学习为现代技术、国际训练标准和超越浪漫的对象，使自己成为城市人。自然爱好者不钓鱼也不打猎；那些是乡村人的活动。他们探索、研究、征服和欣赏自然。在此过程中，他们创造了一套城乡区分。在本节开头我引用的采访轶事中，一位自然爱好者告诉我，她在面对乡村日常生活条件时的厌恶与排斥感（abjection）。通过这种排斥感，她把自己变成祖国的陌生人；她以世界主义旅行者的老练、资源和疏离感接近乡村。这是一个阶级形成过程。通过这些文化区分，一个世界主义的管理阶级塑造了自己。

One of Norman Edwin’s most compelling series of articles concerns a seventeen-year-old high school student who was lost on Mount Kerinci, the highest mountain in Sumatra (Edwin 1990c, 1990d). Yudha Sentika had climbed the peak with six of his school friends. The fog was dense, and the wind was strong. Yudha snapped a photo of his friends at the peak and immediately started down. By the time his friends realized he had gone ahead, he had disappeared into the fog. They themselves couldn’t find the trail. With difficulty, they maneuvered back to the base camp, but Yudha never arrived.
诺曼·埃德温最引人注目的系列文章之一，讲述一名17岁高中学生在苏门答腊最高峰克里奇山迷路的故事（Edwin 1990c, 1990d）。尤达·森蒂卡与六位学校朋友一起攀登该峰。雾很浓，风很大。尤达在峰顶给朋友们拍了张照片，然后立即下撤。等朋友们意识到他先行出发时，他已经消失在雾中。他们自己也找不到小径。他们艰难地回到大本营，但尤达始终没有到达。

Edwin’s first article focuses on the search for Yudha. Nearby residents and members of the local village safety squad began looking for him the next day. “This was well meant, indeed,” Edwin writes. “But, alas, good intentions that are not guided by knowledge and the skill to look for a lost person in the mountains resulted in the fact that their effort had no immediate results” (1990c: 2). This is a mild rebuff compared to what follows. The searchers, ordinary local people without training, were incompetent. Their uncoordinated search muddied the trail for subsequent searches, destroying the possibility of finding footprints or other traces. They allowed rumors to circulate, spreading false information, such as the idea that Yudha’s shirt and water bottle had been found, or worse yet, that he himself had been sighted at a location scores of kilometers distant. The searchers huddled in their tents, confused. Meanwhile, they knew that the boy had no preparations for surviving in the wild. The situation was serious.

埃德温的第一篇文章聚焦于寻找尤达。附近居民和当地村庄安全队成员第二天开始寻找他。“这确实是好意，”埃德温写道。“但唉，没有知识和技能指导的善意，使他们在山中寻找失踪者的努力没有立即结果”（1990c: 2）。与接下来发生的事相比，这是温和的责备。搜寻者是普通当地人，没有受过训练，无法胜任。他们不协调的搜寻搅乱了小径，破坏了后续搜寻发现脚印或其他痕迹的可能性。他们任由谣言传播，散布错误信息，例如尤达的衬衫和水瓶已被找到，或更糟的是，他本人在数十公里外某处被看见。搜寻者蜷缩在帐篷里，不知所措。与此同时，他们知道男孩没有在荒野中生存的准备。情况很严重。

Only during the second week were student nature lovers called in to help. The students, trained in up-to-date search and rescue techniques, came from Jakarta and Padang. They joined with an amateur radio operators’ club to arrange proper communication. And they turned the search around, providing a clear structure and organization and precise work descriptions for volunteers from the closer cities of Jambi and Medan. Teams were deployed with exact directions and the directive to work with all due speed. Edwin’s description (1990c) is illustrated with a photograph showing the nature lovers studying maps, with the following caption: “CLOSE STUDY: The search was carried out with close study and planning. Maps were deployed and data assembled to ascertain approximately where Yudha was lost.” The next photograph, showing a tent just below the peak, is captioned: “CONTROL: Camp 3 (at 3,675 meters) was erected as the control center for the search operation. It is assumed that Yudha split off from his party near this location.” Yet even with radio equipment and precise locational information, the search was not easy. The fog was still thick and the wind strong. “Sometimes we only advanced half a kilometer in a day, because the forest clumps at the base of the peak were so thick,” explained one nature lover to Edwin. One search team was lost in the forest for five days. Edwin documents the ways the mainly male search parties kept up their spirits, from imagining food orders to admiring pin-up calendar girls. They used their radio link to find out the results of international soccer matches, and to bet with other team members on the various foreign teams. Yet after all this, Yudha was not found. Where had he disappeared? Edwin ends his article in English: “The answer, my friend, is blowing in the wind.”
Those of his readers themselves nature lovers, who tend to be avid fans of U.S. popular music, would surely understand the cosmopolitan sadness of the folksong.

直到第二周，学生自然爱好者才被请来帮忙。这些学生受过最新搜救技术训练，来自雅加达和巴东。他们与一个业余无线电操作员俱乐部联合安排适当通信。他们扭转了搜寻局面，为来自较近城市占碑和棉兰的志愿者提供了明确的结构、组织和精确的工作描述。队伍带着准确指令和全速工作的要求被部署。埃德温的描述（1990c）配有一张照片，显示自然爱好者研究地图，标题是：“仔细研究：搜寻在仔细研究与规划下进行。地图被展开，数据被汇集，以确定尤达大致失踪的位置。”下一张照片显示峰顶下方的一个帐篷，标题是：“控制：第三营（海拔3,675米）被设立为搜寻行动的控制中心。据推测，尤达在此地点附近与队伍分开。”然而，即使有无线电设备和精确位置信息，搜寻也不容易。雾仍然浓，风仍然大。“有时我们一天只前进半公里，因为峰顶下方的树丛太密，”一位自然爱好者向埃德温解释。一支搜寻队在森林中迷路五天。埃德温记录了主要由男性组成的搜寻队如何保持士气，从想象食物订单到欣赏挂历女郎。他们用无线电联系了解国际足球比赛结果，并与其他队员就各支外国球队打赌。然而，这一切之后，尤达仍未被找到。他消失到哪里去了？埃德温用英语结束文章：“答案，我的朋友，在风中飘荡。”
他的读者中那些本身就是自然爱好者的人，往往是美国流行音乐的热心歌迷，必定能理解这首民歌中的世界主义悲伤。

In a second article (1990d), Edwin documents the interference the nature lovers felt from a second kind of searcher: traditional healers, dukun, who also came up the mountain to find Yudha. The article suggests that the nature lovers have ambivalent feelings toward what they imagine as traditional, locally rooted, mystic practices. Half-jokingly, they admit to similarities with these searchers by calling them sarkun, from SAR (search and rescue) plus kun (dukun), or dupala, du (dukun) plus pala (short for pencinta alam, nature lover). Yet, Edwin writes, they are embarrassed by these countrymen, who burn incense and sacrifice chickens to ask the spirit inhabitants of the mountain to return Yudha or his corpse. They have come, Edwin speculates, because a rumor has gone out that a Rp. 5 million reward is being offered for finding Yudha; they want the money. They are hypocrites, says one Jakarta nature lover, watching a dukun leave the head of a chicken for the spirits, while taking the body home to eat. They are fools who come up with excuses for why their magical rites do not work. They make irrational requests, asking the nature lovers to plant nodes of yellow bamboo across the mountain. They make the rational-minded nature lovers tense and irritable with their mystical practices. Worse yet, some are brought to the mountain by armed thugs who demand modern equipment, such as walkie-talkies, from the nature lovers.

在第二篇文章（1990d）中，埃德温记录了自然爱好者感到来自另一类搜寻者的干扰：传统治疗师 dukun，他们也上山寻找尤达。文章表明自然爱好者对他们想象为传统的、扎根地方的秘法实践怀有矛盾情感。他们半开玩笑地承认与这些搜寻者相似，称他们 sarkun，即 SAR（搜救）加 kun（dukun），或 dupala，du 加 pala（pencinta alam 的缩写，自然爱好者）。然而，埃德温写道，他们对这些同胞感到尴尬：他们烧香、献鸡，请求山中精灵居民归还尤达或他的尸体。埃德温推测，他们来是因为有传言说找到尤达可获500万印尼盾赏金；他们想要钱。看到一个 dukun 把鸡头留给精灵、却把鸡身带回家吃，一位雅加达自然爱好者说，他们是伪君子。他们是愚蠢的，会为自己的法术为何不灵找借口。他们提出不合理要求，让自然爱好者在山间插黄竹节。他们的神秘实践让理性思维的自然爱好者紧张烦躁。更糟的是，有些人是被武装暴徒带上山的，暴徒向自然爱好者索要现代装备，如对讲机。

Despite all these reasons to dismiss them, the nature lovers find themselves imagining that mystical practices might work. “All methods can be tried when hope is lost,” writes Edwin. “The search and rescue operation, which was full of calculation and based on a healthy rationality, suddenly was infiltrated with dukun practices that were difficult to accept with a fully conscious intellect” (1990d: 2). He quotes the SAR mission coordinator, who spoke for many team members: “Whether you believe it or don’t believe it,” he says, lapsing into Jakarta slang, “I’ve also felt susceptible to black magic” (ibid.). Edwin tells of how the nature lovers’ SAR operations became tinged with magical practices, such as the idea that all search teams must have an even number of members, since Yudha’s unlucky party had an odd number. Worse yet, some search teams started to practice inexplicable rituals, such as sweeping the earth at the edge of the forest while putting a leaf behind the right ear. At the end of the article he returns to the tension between the dukun and the nature lovers, which sometimes resulted in open hostility. Yet he adds a final coda to his report: “It is only necessary to record these facts. So far, the methods cited above have not been proved true. Who knows about another time!” (ibid.). His studied objectivity underlines the ambivalence about traditional mysticism that he shares with most nature lovers.

尽管有所有这些理由轻视他们，自然爱好者却发现自己想象神秘实践也许有效。“希望破灭时，一切方法都可以尝试，”埃德温写道。“充满计算、基于健康理性的搜救行动，突然被 dukun 实践渗透，而这些实践是清醒理智难以接受的”（1990d: 2）。他引用搜救任务协调人的话，后者代表许多队员说：“不管你信不信，”他忽然说起雅加达俚语，“我也觉得自己容易受黑魔法影响”（同上）。埃德温讲述自然爱好者的搜救行动如何带上神秘实践色彩，例如所有搜寻队必须有偶数成员，因为尤达那支倒霉的队伍是奇数。更糟的是，一些搜寻队开始实行无法解释的仪式，例如在森林边缘扫地时把一片叶子放在右耳后。文章末尾，他回到 dukun 与自然爱好者之间的紧张关系，这种紧张有时导致公开敌意。然而他在报告最后加了一段尾声：“只需记录这些事实。到目前为止，上述方法尚未被证明有效。谁知道另一个时候呢！”（同上）。他刻意保持的客观性，强调了他与大多数自然爱好者共有的对传统神秘主义的矛盾心理。

I encountered this set of articles in a Yogya nature lovers’ club office, where the nature lovers showed them to me to illustrate the conversation they were having about “paranormal” and “supernatural” events they had witnessed while out exploring nature. In their conversation, the occurrence of such events was a reasonable topic of debate: Some students declared not to believe in such things; some had not witnessed them but felt they were real, “whether you believe in them or not”; others had first-hand experience with forces they believed to be outside of ordinary rationality (penalaran; masuk akal). Despite these disagreements, the students appeared equally comfortable drawing lines between the rational and the irrational. Their discussion suggested that their ordinary lives were explicable by reason; they thus knew how to identify inexplicable events in the untamed wild that could not be explained by reason—and these were properly captured, they implied, in the ideas and practices of dukun healers, traditional mystics, and village customary beliefs. The very definitiveness of this codification of the supernatural made it possible for them to approach the subject from a distance, as questioning skeptics. Unlike rural people, they implied, they knew better than to mix and confound the ordinary and the mystical. Their ambivalence about the supernatural constituted it as a shadow world—behind ordinary rationality—that they could explore with either respect or playful doubt. And the terms of this ambivalence were proof, to themselves, of the distance they had traveled from village tradition.

我在日惹一个自然爱好者俱乐部办公室偶然看到这组文章，自然爱好者把它们拿给我看，以说明他们正在进行的关于在自然中探索时目睹的“超常”和“超自然”事件的对话。在他们的对话中，这类事件的发生是一个合理的辩论话题：一些学生宣称不相信这类事情；一些人没有目睹过，但觉得它们是真的，“不管你信不信”；另一些人亲身经历过他们认为超出普通理性（penalaran；masuk akal）的力量。尽管有这些分歧，学生们在理性与非理性之间划界时似乎同样自在。他们的讨论表明，他们的日常生活可由理性解释；因此他们知道如何识别未驯服荒野中无法用理性解释的事件——他们暗示，这些事件被恰当地捕捉在 dukun 治疗师、传统神秘主义者和乡村习惯信仰的观念与实践中。正是这种对超自然进行分类的明确性，使他们能够以质疑的怀疑者身份从远处接近这个主题。他们暗示，与乡村人不同，他们更懂得不要把普通与神秘混为一谈。他们对超自然的矛盾心理把它构成一个影子世界——在普通理性背后——他们可以带着尊重或戏谑的怀疑去探索。而这种矛盾心理的措辞，对他们自己来说，证明了他们已远离乡村传统。

As in late Victorian England, debates about the existence of the supernatural deepen the chasm between city and countryside by formulating the grounds of urban difference. When the supernatural is seen as rural and traditional, to argue about it, even as an advocate, establishes one’s metropolitan credentials. Certainly these Yogya students, absorbed in learning the latest scientific methods for appreciating nature, could afford to look back at the countryside with wonderment as well as superiority. In their imaginations at least, they were bound for a future in which their cosmopolitan expertise would allow them a combination of disdain and nostalgia about rural society.
如同维多利亚晚期英格兰，关于超自然存在的辩论通过阐述城市差异的基础，加深城乡鸿沟。当超自然被视为乡村的、传统的，争论它——即使作为拥护者——也确立了一个人的大都市资格。当然，这些日惹学生沉浸在最新科学自然欣赏方法的学习中，可以带着惊奇和优越感回望乡村。至少在他们的想象中，他们正走向一个未来，其世界主义专长将让他们对乡村社会同时抱有轻蔑与怀旧。

During trekking, you’ll up and down the mountain chain, cross some rivers and hanging bridges, caves, waterfall and a great variety of flora and fauna with a beautiful panorama. Advisable you must take licensed tour guide, porter and a good personal equipment.
徒步期间，你将上下穿越山脉，越过河流和吊桥，经过洞穴和瀑布，见到丰富的动植物与美丽风光。建议你必须聘请持证导游和搬运工，并携带良好的个人装备。
—from Come Experience to South Kalimantan, tour pamphlet
——摘自《来体验南加里曼丹》（Come Experience to South Kalimantan），旅游宣传册

After graduating from college, some nature lovers establish outdoor adventure clubs, through which they can become tour guides and activities facilitators for domestic and international tourists. I talked to the founder and some of the members of one such group in Banjarmasin, South Kalimantan, in 1997. They offered me the English-language tour brochure from which I have quoted above, and they urged me to send American travelers to them. So far, they admitted, they had had no success in finding international trekkers to guide. However, they were organizing trips for Indonesian trekkers from other parts of the country. Indeed, it seemed that their determination to attract international trekkers was an indirect route to organizing domestic trekkers. Indonesian nature lovers want to go to internationally attractive places. To make the jungles of South Kalimantan a prime destination for Indonesian students, the group felt it necessary to promote the area as an international destination—and, indeed, to advertise it in English; if international visitors showed up as well, so much the better. But most of the adventure visits in the 1990s came from domestic tourism.

大学毕业后，一些自然爱好者建立户外冒险俱乐部，借此成为国内和国际游客的导游与活动组织者。1997年，我在南加里曼丹班贾尔马辛与这样一个团体的创始人和一些成员交谈。他们给了我上面引用的英文旅游手册，并敦促我把美国旅行者介绍给他们。他们承认，到目前为止他们还没成功找到可接待的国际徒步者。然而，他们正在为来自全国其他地区的印尼徒步者组织旅行。事实上，他们吸引国际徒步者的决心似乎是组织国内徒步者的间接途径。印尼自然爱好者想去具有国际吸引力的地方。为了让南加里曼丹的丛林成为印尼学生的首选目的地，这个团体觉得有必要把该地区宣传为国际目的地——而且用英语做广告；如果国际游客也出现，那就更好。但20世纪90年代大多数冒险访问来自国内旅游。

Nature loving has domesticated international adventure tourism in Indonesia, that is, it has turned its dreams and destinations into sites for Indonesian national experience. Foreign adventurers still come to tackle Indonesia’s jungles, rivers, caves, and mountains—and most continue to organize their trips through international channels and thus avoid contact with Indonesian nature lovers. Yet there are few wild spots in the country that have not been thoroughly challenged by Indonesians. The most active clubs mount expeditions all over the country. Enthusiastic individuals have visited many places across the archipelago. Here is one young man’s list of the adventure and training trips he took with his Yogya nature lovers’ club:
自然之爱在印尼驯化了国际冒险旅游，也就是说，它把其梦想和目的地变成印尼国家经验的场所。外国冒险者仍来挑战印尼的丛林、河流、洞穴和山脉——而且大多数人继续通过国际渠道组织旅行，从而避免与印尼自然爱好者接触。然而，这个国家很少有荒野地点没被印尼人彻底挑战过。最活跃的俱乐部在全国各地发起探险。热情的个人访问了群岛许多地方。以下是一位年轻男子与日惹自然爱好者俱乐部一起进行的冒险和训练旅行清单：
洛雷林杜，苏拉威西，1989（探索）
默拉皮、默尔巴布、苏明、孙多罗、斯拉梅特，1990–93（攀登）
瓜拉库伦，加里曼丹，1991（训练领队）
梅鲁贝蒂里，爪哇，1991（训练领队）
塔西克马拉亚，爪哇，1991（训练领队）
巴唐阿赛，苏门答腊，1992（漂流）

Despite this profusion of places, I never heard nature lovers boast of their acquisition of various sites, in the way international tourists do all the time. (“I have been to Sulawesi, and I am on my way to Kalimantan.”) Although club members could recite lists of their expeditions, the places themselves seemed unimportant except as sites for experiencing a rather generic untamed nature. Some nature lovers have fond memories of the challenge of travel in parts of the country with which they were previously unfamiliar. One young Javanese woman told me of her journey to climb a mountain on the island of Lombok by herself. She knew no one there, but she dressed in bulky clothing, rather like a man, to avoid harassment, and she was happily able to get directions from local people. Although the unfamiliarity of the place plays into her story of bravery and loneliness, it was not Lombok as a place that impressed her, but the wild beauty of mountain scenery: a hidden lake; a stretch of loose gravel that made it almost impossible to climb; a vast panorama. This was nature that transcended place. The adventure tourism of nature lovers differs in this way from the international tourism it follows: It does not sponsor a calculating accumulation of places, condensed into short, harrowing experiences that seem, to the tourist, to “capture” the meaning of the site. Instead, it is the distinction between home and the wild that is reiterated in these domestic tours. The trips affirm the homogeneity of the Indonesian nation even as they separate it into cosmopolitan centers and wild peripheries.

尽管地点如此丰富，我从未听到自然爱好者像国际游客那样不断吹嘘自己征服了各个地点。（“我去过苏拉威西，正要去加里曼丹。”）虽然俱乐部成员能背诵他们的探险清单，但地点本身似乎不重要，除了作为体验一种相当普遍的未驯服自然的场所。一些自然爱好者对该国先前不熟悉地区旅行的挑战怀有美好记忆。一位年轻的爪哇女子告诉我她独自去龙目岛爬山的旅程。她在那里谁也不认识，但她穿着臃肿的衣服，很像男人，以避免骚扰，并且愉快地从当地人那里得到方向指引。虽然这个地方的陌生感助长了她的勇敢与孤独故事，但给她留下印象的不是作为地方的龙目岛，而是山景的荒野之美：一个隐藏的湖；一段几乎无法攀爬的松散砾石；一片广阔全景。这是超越地方的自然。自然爱好者的冒险旅游以这种方式不同于它所追随的国际旅游：它不鼓励对地点的计算式积累，把地点压缩成短暂、惊险的体验，让游客觉得“捕捉”了该地点的意义。相反，在这些国内旅行中反复强调的是家与荒野之间的区分。这些旅行肯定印尼这个国家的同质性，即使它们把这个国家分为世界主义中心和荒野边缘。

Nature lovers’ expeditions involve research as well as adventure. Common kinds of research include surveys of vegetation or wildlife, as well as ethnographic surveys of “local people” (masyarakat sekitar). Most of the places that nature lovers explore have already been mapped by foreign and domestic surveyors. Still, survey research connects nature lovers with conventions of militarized science, including the science of colonial conquest and centralized state administration. The “local people” are further localized and contained by imagining them as objects of scientific inquiry; the researchers emerge, in contrast, as cosmopolitan travelers. The nature lovers take notes; the local people can merely answer questions. Yet this form of objectification can also, sometimes, lead to moments of identification. Those nature lovers who became political activists almost always spoke of learning about the social problems of the countryside from talking to village people during their nature lover trips. For example, a nature lovers’ club in Banjarmasin told me how they traveled to the east coast of Kalimantan to check out caves as possible sites for exploration. The area they chose was being claimed by a coal mining company, and the local people were angry that they had received no compensation for their land; meanwhile, problems of erosion and pollution loomed. The nature lovers’ club decided to form an advocacy group on the issue of mining. They hosted several informative seminars on the topic and joined with Jakarta-based activists to lobby the provincial government to consider social issues. In part due to their efforts, Banjarmasin became a center of mining activism.

自然爱好者的探险既包含研究，也包含冒险。常见研究包括植被或野生动物调查，以及对“当地人”（masyarakat sekitar）的民族志调查。自然爱好者探索的大多数地方，早已被外国和本国测量员绘制成图。尽管如此，调查研究仍把自然爱好者与军事化科学的惯例联系起来，包括殖民征服的科学和中央集权国家行政的科学。“当地人”被进一步地方化并加以限制，因为他们被想象为科学探究的对象；相比之下，研究者以世界主义旅行者的身份出现。自然爱好者记笔记；当地人只能回答问题。然而这种客体化形式有时也会导向认同时刻。那些成为政治活动家的自然爱好者几乎总是谈到，他们在自然爱好者旅行中通过与村民交谈，了解到乡村的社会问题。例如，班贾尔马辛的一个自然爱好者俱乐部告诉我，他们如何前往加里曼丹东海岸查看洞穴，作为可能的探险地点。他们选中的地区正被一家煤矿公司圈占，当地人因未获得土地补偿而愤怒；与此同时，侵蚀和污染问题逼近。该自然爱好者俱乐部决定就采矿问题成立一个倡导团体。他们就该议题举办了几次信息研讨会，并与雅加达的活动家联手，游说省政府考虑社会问题。部分由于他们的努力，班贾尔马辛成为围绕采矿问题开展行动的中心。

Whether participants emerge as activists or merely as admirers of wild beauty, their expeditions remap national geography. Nature lovers offer a new cosmopolitan standard with which to separate Indonesian centers and peripheries: the wildness of alam bebas, untamed nature, becomes a form of peripheral “difference” that defines through contrast the worldly order of centers. Unlike other Indonesian measuring sticks of urban-rural contrast—such as “development,” “modernity,” or status hierarchy—this is a geography that allows for romance, inspiration, and advocacy as well as exoticization.
无论参与者最终成为活动家，还是仅仅成为荒野之美的欣赏者，他们的探险都重新绘制了国家地理。自然爱好者提供了一种新的世界主义标准，用来区分印尼的中心与边缘：未被驯服的自然 alam bebas 的野性，成为一种边缘“差异”，通过对比界定了中心的世界性秩序。不同于印尼其他城乡对比的尺度——如“发展”“现代性”或地位等级——这是一种允许浪漫、灵感、倡导以及异域化并存的地理。

It is a geography that can only be maintained by the identification of Indonesian nature lovers and international travelers. This identification is furthered by the fact that a few nature lovers do get the chance to explore wild nature abroad. Even these few set the sights for the many who stay closer to home. For example, the nature lovers’ club of the University of Indonesia sent representatives in 1990 to climb a mountain in Russia. The trip was joined by none other than Norman Edwin, whose newspaper report inspired other nature lovers—including the ones who showed the article to me—to imagine themselves in foreign climes (Edwin 1990e). Edwin’s article suggests not only the force of foreign travel in reaffirming cosmopolitanism, but also the self-conscious openness of Indonesian nature loving to influences from the histories of international adventure sports.

这是一种只有通过印尼自然爱好者与国际旅行者的认同才能维持的地理。少数自然爱好者确实有机会出国探索野生自然，这进一步强化了这种认同。即使这少数人也为更多留在国内的人设定目标。例如，1990年，印尼大学自然爱好者俱乐部派代表去俄罗斯攀登一座山。参加这次旅行的正是诺曼·埃德温；他的报纸报道激励其他自然爱好者——包括那些把文章拿给我看的人——想象自己身处异国（Edwin 1990e）。埃德温的文章不仅表明国外旅行在重申世界主义方面的力量，也表明印尼自然之爱自觉地对国际冒险运动史中的影响保持开放。

The team went to what was then the Soviet Union to climb Mount Ebrus, the highest mountain in Europe. The mountain had only recently been opened to international climbers; the Indonesian team joined a cosmopolitan group in re-claiming the mountain for the world. The team was inspired, too, because in earlier years the mountain had been a center of the development of international mountain climbing as a sport. It had been used as a training area for ascents to Mt. Everest, and it was also a destination on its own. Edwin describes the 1920s as the “golden era” of international mountain climbing there. In the 1930s, a Soviet climbing sensibility had developed, beginning a period in which more than 600,000 “Soviet alpinists” trained for this “master sport.”

队伍前往当时的苏联攀登欧洲最高峰厄尔布鲁士山（Mount Ebrus）。这座山最近才向国际登山者开放；印尼队伍加入一个世界主义团体，重新为世界认领这座山。队伍也受到激励，因为早年这座山一直是国际登山运动发展的中心。它曾被用作攀登珠穆朗玛峰训练的场地，本身也是一个目的地。埃德温把20世纪20年代描述为那里国际登山的“黄金时代”。20世纪30年代，一种苏联登山意识发展起来，开启了一个超过60万“苏联登山家”为这项“大师运动”受训的时期。

The Indonesian nature lovers’ expedition—following international expectations of the mountain’s challenge—required teamwork and self-sacrifice for its success. One of the four team members was struck with severe mountain sickness, and Edwin himself fell ill with altitude-induced pulmonary edema; they had to be evacuated to lower elevations. But they urged the other two team members to continue, and they reached the peak. From there they could inspire nature lovers across Indonesia.
印尼自然爱好者探险队遵循国际对这座山挑战的期待，需要团队合作与自我牺牲才能成功。四名队员中有一人患严重高山症，埃德温本人也因高原引起的肺水肿病倒；他们必须被撤到较低海拔。但他们敦促另外两名队员继续前进，那两人登上了顶峰。从那里，他们可以激励全印尼的自然爱好者。
Nor was Norman Edwin defeated by his failure to reach the peak. He continued to climb mountains, foreign and domestic. In 1992, he died in an attempt to scale a peak in Argentina.
诺曼·埃德温也没有因未能登顶而一蹶不振。他继续攀登国内外山峰。1992年，他在尝试攀登阿根廷一座山峰时去世。
Hundreds of meters high, hanging from a cliff! Are you brave enough with a single rope? Prove you have the daring!
数百米高，悬挂在崖壁上！只凭一根绳子，你有足够的勇气吗？证明你有胆量！
——1997年印尼各地可见的万宝路香烟广告

Before Norman Edwin died, he made a different sort of national impression. He signed a contract with Gudang Garam, Indonesia’s largest cigarette manufacturer, to become a cigarette advertising model. Gudang Garam billboards showed him on a mountain peak; as one nature lover quipped, he was posed somewhere in Jakarta, but the photograph was made to look as if he was climbing in West Papua. When Edwin died, there was an outpouring of sentiment, and Gudang Garam, in respect for his memory, agreed to take the billboards down. Soon, however, they had picked another mountain climber model. I remember him on billboards across Indonesia in 1994, standing on top of a high rock with a roll of rope over his arm that placed him somewhere between a climbers’ exercise and Marlboro country. Soon, too, another Indonesian company had picked up the theme of adventures in nature. Bentoel cigarettes began advertising with the slogan: “I love the blue of Indonesia” and photographs of river-running sports. (“Blue” also referred to the cigarette pack’s color.)

在诺曼·埃德温去世之前，他给人留下了另一种全国性印象。他与印尼最大香烟制造商古当加拉姆（Gudang Garam）签约，成为香烟广告模特。古当加拉姆的广告牌展示他站在山峰上；正如一位自然爱好者打趣说，他其实是在雅加达某处摆姿势，但照片被弄得看起来像是在西巴布亚攀登。埃德温去世后，人们纷纷表达哀思，古当加拉姆为尊重其纪念，同意撤下广告牌。然而，他们很快又选了另一位登山者模特。我记得1994年他出现在印尼各地的广告牌上，站在高岩顶上，手臂上搭着一卷绳子，使他处于攀岩者训练与万宝路之乡之间的某个位置。很快，另一家印尼公司也接过了自然冒险的主题。本托埃尔（Bentoel）香烟开始用“我爱印尼的蓝”这一口号，以及江河漂流运动的照片做广告。（“蓝”也指该香烟包装的颜色。）

Some time before this, nature loving had established itself as a small but distinctive market niche for urban youth. There was room for small-scale entrepreneurship in the making and marketing of daypacks, camp stoves, and rock climbing grommets. However, the market status of nature lovers expanded wildly with their entry into the cigarette advertising business; now their image was selling one of the country’s more profitable products. The idea of nature loving became available at an entirely new level: Every cigarette smoker could imagine him- or herself a nature lover. The commercial lineage of nature loving brought a new national notoriety and a new way to become cosmopolitan through the fantasy of fulfilled consumption. No company proved better at working this fantasy than Philip Morris, the makers of Marlboro cigarettes.

在此之前的某个时候，自然之爱已经确立为城市青年一个虽小但独特的市场利基。在日间背包、露营炉和攀岩环扣的制造与营销中，小规模创业仍有空间。然而，随着自然爱好者进入香烟广告业，他们的市场地位急剧扩大；现在他们的形象在推销这个国家利润更丰厚的产品之一。自然之爱的观念在一个全新层面变得可得：每个吸烟者都能想象自己是自然爱好者。自然之爱的商业谱系带来新的全国性名声，也带来一种通过实现消费的幻想成为世界主义者的新方式。没有哪家公司比万宝路的制造商菲利普·莫里斯更善于经营这种幻想。

In the 1980s and 1990s, Philip Morris had embarked on an ambitious globalization campaign (Barnet and Cavanaugh 1994: 184-207). Earlier in the century, the company had focused on selling cigarettes in the United States. But by the 1980s, U.S. cigarette health warnings and tobacco industry regulation had alerted the company to the need to expand its sights. The company bought up grocery and household product makers and distributors; still, cigarettes remained their most profitable product. Watching rates of smoking drop among middle-class white Americans, they moved to target other groups of smokers: both minorities in the United States and the people of Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

20世纪80和90年代，菲利普·莫里斯展开一场雄心勃勃的全球化运动（Barnet and Cavanaugh 1994: 184–207）。该世纪早些时候，公司专注于在美国销售香烟。但到20世纪80年代，美国的香烟健康警告和烟草业监管让公司意识到需要扩大眼界。它收购了食品杂货与家用产品制造商和分销商；不过香烟仍是其利润最高的产品。看到美国中产白人吸烟率下降，公司转向其他吸烟群体：美国少数族裔，以及亚洲、非洲和拉丁美洲的人民。

Breaking into these markets was not simple. Many Asian countries controlled the importation of cigarettes, protecting the profits of domestic cigarette manufacturers. During the 1980s, Philip Morris took an aggressive stance against such protection, working together with then U.S. President Reagan’s trade representative, Clayton Yeutter, to dismantle protective barriers against Marlboro. Yuetter used a U.S. trade regulation that allows punitive action against nations that practice “discriminatory” trade restrictions against U.S. exporters to attack the trade regulations of Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, forcing each, in turn, to capitulate to U.S. cigarette companies. Thus, for example, the United States forced Taiwan to eliminate its tariffs on foreign cigarettes in 1988; within one year foreign imports had taken 21 percent of the market (Barnet and Cavanaugh 1994: 202). With the assistance of the U.S. government, Philip Morris was able to make its product popular across Asia.

打入这些市场并不简单。许多亚洲国家管制香烟进口，保护国内烟草制造商的利润。20世纪80年代，菲利普·莫里斯对这类保护采取强硬立场，与当时美国总统里根的贸易代表克莱顿·尤特（Clayton Yeutter）合作，拆除针对万宝路的保护壁垒。尤特利用一项美国贸易法规——该法规允许对实行“歧视性”贸易限制、针对美国出口商的国家采取惩罚性行动——来打击日本、台湾和韩国的贸易法规，迫使它们依次向美国烟草公司让步。例如，美国在1988年迫使台湾取消对外国香烟的关税；一年之内，外国进口烟就占据了21%的市场（Barnet and Cavanaugh 1994: 202）。在美国政府的协助下，菲利普·莫里斯使其产品风靡亚洲。

Philip Morris has always relied heavily on advertising. Introduced in 1954, the Marlboro man—the virile cowboy smoker—was an immediate success (Barnet and Cavanagh 1994: 189-95). The banning of cigarette advertising from U.S. television in 1970 worked to the advantage of the Marlboro man, whose celebration of freedom in the Great Outdoors looked particularly good on billboards. While company executives feel strongly that the Marlboro man has “global” appeal, they have also invested heavily in market research that makes the Marlboro image more appropriate to particular national markets. In Hong Kong, for example, the cowboy looked to local people like a menial worker; Philip Morris removed him but kept the horse, an appealing image for Chinese consumers.
